nodes.text: AD 491–512. PASCHASIUS THE DEACON.
PROLEGOMENON.
(From Cave.)

Paschasius, deacon of the Roman Church, flourished at the beginning of this century, in the year 501. When the Roman schism flared up in the year 498, he vigorously defended the party of Laurentius against Symmachus, and he stubbornly championed his cause right up to his death. He died in the year 512. In connection with this, Gregory, or whoever the author of the Dialogues is, tells us a quite charming tale about the soul of Paschasius being burned in the flames of Purgatory. There survives a Letter of Paschasius to Eugippius, prefixed to the Life of St Severinus, in Surius under 8 January and in Baronius under the year 496. There are also two Books on the Holy Spirit, against Macedonius, Cologne, 1539, in octavo; Helmstedt, 1613; and in the Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. VIII, p. 806. Casimir Oudin flatly denies that these are by Paschasius, and contends that they should be attributed to Faustus of Riez. Certainly his reasons, which can be seen in his own work, Supplement, p. 107, do not seem altogether to be despised. Yet since these most choice and brilliant books (to use Gregory's words) rest on the testimony of Gregory, who expressly attributes them to Paschasius the deacon (and Oudin himself acknowledges that the authority of the Dialogues in this matter is very great), to say nothing now of Sigebert of Gembloux (ch. 17), they are not to be taken away from our Paschasius rashly. Nor do the titles of certain manuscripts stand in the way, since these, added through the carelessness of copyists, quite often deceive unwary readers; especially since Gennadius (ch. 85) records that Faustus wrote a book on the Holy Spirit. And Trithemius himself, whom Oudin cites as a witness on his side, clearly ascribes to our Paschasius these very books which Gregory mentions; although, while dealing with something else, he carelessly attached the opening words of this work to the single book which Faustus wrote on this subject.
THE TWO BOOKS OF PASCHASIUS THE DEACON ON THE HOLY SPIRIT.
PREFACE.

The catholic faith has been spread through the whole world by the patriarchs and prophets and the dispensers of grace, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Apostolic care and perfection, just as it had spread this faith abroad through the holy pages, so gathered it together with wonderful brevity in the saving [formula] of the Creed, and arranged it into one body as if out of diverse kinds of remedies, and as it were made from countless spices a precious ointment, whose fragrance has filled all the ends of the earth with the power of its spiritual sweetness, so that in its very rise over the whole world the strength of the truth may appear. And since we must, for those who go astray, as for little children and the ignorant, go back over the first elements of the Christian tradition (on these see Ambrose, On Abraham, book I, ch. a, and Prudentius' Psychomachia), in this perfect form of the Creed both the unity and the trinity are plainly disclosed, since the confession, repeated three times, to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, renders one homage of belief. In these words also the three hundred and eighteen, the sacred number of bishops, condemned the errors of Arius and Macedonius as they emerged, saying: I believe in God the Father, I believe in his only Son our Lord, I believe also in the Holy Spirit. For even if the weakness of a few from this number fell away, it did not undo the mystery of the number as a whole. And we have called it a sacred number for this reason: that three hundred, in the Greek reckoning of numerals, shows the sign of the cross, and eighteen the adorable name of Jesus. In this mystery of number, then, in which holy Abraham too triumphed over countless nations, the piety of the elders confounds the enemy of the faith under the one proclamation of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. From this it is also to be understood that those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit [are] under eternal damnation, either as baptized without the profession of the Creed, or as having lied to themselves in that very Creed and font, since every person, renouncing the devil, confesses: I believe also in the Holy Spirit. I believe, I say, also in the Holy Spirit. Let us recognize the special privilege of this very word. Any human being can believe him; but to believe in him, know that you owe this to the divine majesty alone. But this too is a further point: it is one thing to believe that God exists, another to believe in God. Even the devil is said to believe that God exists, according to the Apostle: For even the demons believe and tremble. But no one is shown to believe in God unless he has hoped in him with devotion. To believe in God, then, is this: to seek him faithfully, [that] is to pass over into him with all one's love. I believe in him, then, is to say: I confess him, I worship him, I adore him, I hand over and pour my whole self into his right and lordship. In the reverence of this profession is contained all the homage owed to the divine name.
BOOK ONE.
CHAPTER ONE.
That we ought to believe the Catholic Church not 'in' [it] as [we believe] in the Holy Spirit, but with the preposition 'in' removed.

But you object and say that God cannot at once be shown by these words in which we say, I believe also in the Holy Spirit, because there follows: I believe in the holy catholic Church. First, I do not know how Macedonius dares to name the catholic Church, who has been shut out, an exile from salvation, outside the catholic [Church], having become one of the number of those of whom it is said: The wicked walk round about. So you say: I believe in the holy catholic Church. Why do you try, by inserting a tiny [syllable], that is the syllable 'in', to weave in a vast darkness? We believe the Church as the mother of regeneration; we do not believe in the Church as in the author of salvation. For since the whole Church confesses this of the Holy Spirit, can it also believe in itself? Therefore, since one must believe in the Trinity alone in a special sense, as the teaching of the Fathers mentioned, celebrated throughout the whole world, also confirms, either remove this syllable from the name of the Church, or else assert by a clear profession from the Scriptures that you believe in the Church, teach it by testimonies, prove it by divine oracles, setting aside the presumption of your own words. Let us take what is to be believed entirely from the sacred volumes, from whose spring the sequence of the Creed itself has been drawn and stands. Whoever believes in the Church believes in man. Man did not begin from the Church, but the Church began to be from man. Withdraw, therefore, from this blasphemous conviction, that you should think you ought to believe in any human creature, since one must not believe at all either in an angel or in an archangel. For those things which follow the name of the Holy Spirit in the Creed, up to the close of the Creed, are taken with the preposition 'in' removed, so that we believe the holy Church, the communion of saints, the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, eternal life. Let us believe in God, that is, so that we confess that these things have been laid down by God and stand firm in God. For the inexperience of some has dragged and snatched this preposition 'in', as if from the nearest neighbouring clause, into what follows, and has added it superfluously and imprudently. But in none of the canonical [writings], on which the text of the Creed depends, have we received that we ought to believe in the Church as in the Holy Spirit and the Son. And therefore, since every creature is excluded from this honour, he in whom we are commanded to believe is God. This word the voice of the Lord the Saviour assigns specially to divinity, saying thus: Believe in God, and believe in me. And again: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me (John 14:10 and 12).
CHAPTER II.
That Christ was not begotten but created by the Holy Spirit, as being God.

Now since the catholic Church confesses, he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, the Macedonians must be asked at this point whether they consider the Holy Spirit the creator or the father of the Redeemer. If they should answer father, since they have already said at the beginning of the Creed, I believe in God the Father almighty, they will confusedly be confessing that he has two fathers. But if they assert creator, as the truth holds, they will be forced, even by necessity, to declare with us [that he is] God of the universe. And therefore he speaks through the prophet Isaiah, as through his trumpet and from his temple, when he foreshadowed the two substances in Christ: Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the just one; let the earth be opened and bud forth the Saviour; I the Lord have created him (Isa. 45). For the man assumed from Mary was the work of the Holy Spirit, not a portion [of him]; not begotten by him, but created. He was conceived by power, not by substance; by operation, not by participation; by might, not by descent.
CHAPTER III.
On asserting the unity by the testimonies of the prophets.

The catholic faith venerates a threefold majesty under the confession of one divinity. Receive the one divinity from the sacred volumes: Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God (Deut. 6); and: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone; in the psalms: Doing wonders, you alone are God. Again: You alone are most high over all the earth. Through Isaiah also: God of Israel, who sits upon the Cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms of the earth (Isa. 45). Again: I am the Lord, I am the first and the last (Isa. 41). Again: I am the Lord, that is my name; my glory I will not give to another (Isa. 42). But so that you may know that this testimony, that is, the first and the last, pertains to Christ, he said of himself in another place: I am the beginning, who also speak to you (John 8). Again: Before me there was no God, and after me there will be none. I am the Lord, and apart from me there is no Saviour (Isa. 43). This pertains specially to Christ, the Saviour of the human race. Again: Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, and your former from the womb: I am the Lord who makes all things, stretching out the heavens, alone establishing the earth, and no one with me (Isa. 44); this pertains to Jesus, and refers properly to the maker and redeemer. Of whom the evangelist records: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. Again: There is no God any more apart from me, and there is no Saviour besides me (Isa. 45). Again: I am the first and the last; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens (Isa. 48). Just as Jesus Christ in another place plainly asserts of himself, saying: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end (Rev. 21). In these testimonies the Holy Spirit too is contained; in them the unity of the whole substance is to be confessed in such a way that the distinct property of the persons, and an undivided plurality, is also to be believed to be present in them.
CHAPTER IV.
On the Trinity, and that even the liberal disciplines have taken over [the teaching] of three Persons.

Since, then, we have shown the one deity of the Word, let us now teach three in one Deity: three names, not three kingdoms; three designations, but not three powers; three hypostases or subsistences, but not three substances. It is also clear that worldly wisdom understood that the whole multitude of worldly things is enclosed within the scheme of three persons. What are these three? That is: I, You, He. So, as we have said, even the liberal studies, borrowing instruction from the spiritual disciplines, perceived that there are only three persons in things, and it was plainly apparent to them that neither does the second person suffice for completeness nor can the third be exceeded, because fullness, tending towards the third number, shows duality to be half-full, while perfection, completed in three, rejects a fourth. These things, then, having been passed over with a light mention, let us rather assert by sacred testimonies that the Trinity subsists in unity [without] change. But you say: Why do you put before me the words 'unity' and 'Trinity', which you do not find in the canonical reading? It is no wonder if one who does not deserve to enter the inner sanctuary of holy things takes fright at and shrinks back from even the testimony of the truth. For what is so near, so natural, so proper, as that from 'one' 'unity', and from 'three' 'Trinity', should be named, first of all in catholic definitions? Words that depend on what precedes them are not to be examined on their own, nor indeed does it follow that things should be declared foreign which arise from 'one' and 'three', that is, from the proper character of a plain starting point. Note that neither of these terms is presumptuous, but derivative. These words antiquity found from the time of the primitive Church, authority brought forth, and long ages confirmed.
CHAPTER V.
Since the Son is called the face of the Father, he is recognised as coeval with the Father.

Receive the Trinity from the sacred volumes. In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters (Gen. 1). The Father the author, the coeval beginning, the Holy Spirit poured over the waters. So the eminence of the one who rules was borne over the waters, already then, I believe, prefiguring the gifts of baptism. In the making of man too, the threefold repetition of deity shows that it is the work not of one but of three persons. For thus we read: And God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness. Note the statement, single in its proposition, manifold in its response. And God said, let us make man. What else is this but that the substance of the unity speaks, and the power of the Trinity works? Observe how three times the name of God is pronounced in the creation of man. For so we have it in Genesis: And God said, let us make man. And again: God created man. And a third time: God blessed him. God said, God made, God blessed. Because of the three persons, the one divinity is repeated three times. In this place understand plainly the mystery of the Trinity as well. See, the image and likeness of God is given to each man by three, and yet it is recognised to be one. God said, let us make. Pay careful attention: while one speaks and not one makes, and while again he mixes plural with singular, and does not say 'in our images and likenesses', or indeed 'in my image and likeness', he commends the unity by the singular, the trinity by the plural. So in saying: Let us make man in our image, the number of persons is set out; in saying in the singular 'in the image and likeness', the undivided divinity is gathered into one substance. When God had appeared to Abraham at the door of the tent (Gen. 18), and out of one, three had wondrously presented themselves to his eyes, aware of the majesty he worshipped one in three. In the psalm also the unity is plainly designated in its persons: Do not cast me, it says, from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me (Ps. 50). The Son, just as he is understood as the image of the Father, so also as the face of the Father. And therefore we read: Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father too (John 14). And again: Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? Note the mystery of the Trinity in the faith of a perfect confession. The prophet speaks to the Father, professes the Son of the Father as the Father's face, and also professes the Holy Spirit spread through all things. Of the Son, too, the Lord speaks to Moses: My face will go before you (Exod. 33). This name, that is 'face', pertains both to the substance of the unity and to the eternity of the majesty. As for their thinking him lesser because he was born: what is it for God to be born of God, except to have come forth from God by nature? But you say: If he is from him, he is younger. See, the arm is born from the body, and the face from its body, and yet it is agreed that the face is not lesser than its head, nor the arm later than its body. If, then, any head was ever older [than its face], then venture to assert that the Father is older than his image, which consists in the perfect likeness and equality of Christ. So the Son cannot be distinguished from the Father either in power or in time, just as the face cannot be separated from the head, nor can it in any way be found younger than its head.
CHAPTER VI.
That the Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit himself.

But you say: Show me that the Holy Spirit subsists in his own essence. Wherever or however often I read either 'the Spirit of the Father', or 'my Spirit', or 'the Spirit of God', I see, you say, that it is to be referred not to the person of the Holy Spirit but to that of the Father. First, they pile up the blasphemy of their impiety on this, when they say alternately that the Holy Spirit of God is to be believed either a creature or indeed the Father himself. Rightly does one who does not confess the Holy Spirit sink with confused mind even to insulting the Father. Certainly, if [he is] a thing made, he cannot belong to the substance of the Father. But if you think him the Father's power, how do you presume to humble him to the insult of being a thing made? We, however, will show by plain testimonies that 'the Spirit of God' is said not of the Father, but properly of the Holy Spirit. We read in Isaiah that the Holy Spirit of the Lord descended upon the Lord Jesus, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety (Isa. 11). Of this spirit of the Lord, then, who came down upon the Saviour in a sacred descent, the Son says through Isaiah: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me (Isa. 61). And the evangelist Matthew: See, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove (Matt. 3). And this spirit of God, which the Saviour received in baptism, the evangelist Luke clearly taught to be the Holy Spirit, saying: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan (Luke 3). We read in the prophet Joel: In those days I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh (Joel 2). That what he says, 'of my spirit', was said of the Holy Spirit is clear, because when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles at the sacred feast of Pentecost, then the apostle Peter asserted this testimony from the prophet. That this Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit himself the evangelists taught in differing words but with harmonious truth. For when Matthew had said: For it is not you who speak, but the spirit of your Father who speaks in you, Mark plainly explained this spirit of the Father to be the Holy Spirit, saying: Whatever is given to you, that you will speak; for it is not you who are speaking, but the Holy Spirit. And Luke likewise showed this Spirit of God to be the Holy Spirit, saying: Do not be anxious how or what you are to say. For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what you ought to say. According to these things, then, whenever you read either 'the Spirit of the Father' or 'the Spirit of God', you must lay aside your error and confess that it is to be referred specifically to the Holy Spirit. Likewise Isaiah too had proclaimed the Holy Spirit as one in the glory of the Trinity, when he says: I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne, and the seraphim stood and cried one to another: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth (Isa. 6). And afterwards he says: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Go and you will say to this people: Hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not see. Who this Lord of Sabaoth was, who in an assumed form was seen by the prophet or spoke in the prophet, the apostle Paul shows in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: Well did the Holy Spirit speak through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers: Hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not see (Acts, last chapter). Let us at least believe Paul, the most renowned herald of the truth, that the Holy Spirit was that God of hosts whom Isaiah saw, and who spoke through Isaiah. But since [the cry] resounds with a threefold repetition, Holy, holy, holy, let us see whether this honour does not look to the Trinity. Isaiah, when he says: I saw the Lord of Sabaoth, is recognised as preaching the Father to the Jews. John the evangelist is shown plainly to assert the Son, saying thus: Therefore they could not believe in Jesus, because Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart (John 12; Isa. 6). Isaiah said these things when he saw the grace of the Son of God and spoke of him. And as to what the same Isaiah says: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Go and say to this people: seeing you will see and not see — this Lord the apostle Paul, as we have said, confirms to be the Holy Spirit. Do you see, then, that this cry, Holy, holy, holy, celebrates the whole Trinity together? And just as in these three words there is no unlikeness, no difference, so in the truth of the Trinity there can be no disagreement.
CHAPTER VII.
On the finger of God.

But you say: From this the Holy Spirit is recognised to be lesser, because he is called the finger of God. It is not so. But when you hear it said of the Holy Spirit, If I by the Spirit of God, or by the finger of God, cast out demons, know that what is shown is not a lessening of grace but a unity of substance: not a disparity of honour but a concord of work. What then? Because the Holy Spirit is sometimes called a finger, is he therefore sometimes believed to be less than the Son and the Father? Flee the error of this persuasion; see whether this designation 'finger' does not at times include both the Father and the Son. We remember that it was not said of one finger, when we read: For I see your heavens, the works of your fingers. But you say that in 'fingers' only this is signified, the Son and the Holy Spirit, under a kind of duality. Lest you try to assert this of two persons, in another place Isaiah speaks with a number of fingers, naming the Trinity: Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers (Isa. 40)? What is more evident concerning the unity of the Trinity, what clearer? Has he not here, in three fingers, weighed the equality of one power on a kind of balance of mystery? Therefore, as has been said, since you are now instructed concerning the partnership of the work, do not doubt the parity of power. In saying, then, Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers, they mean to speak here specifically of the co-operation of power and of the unity of substance, which is shown to be one and the same in the three fingers. But nonetheless observe in Isaiah the proper person of the Holy Spirit, within the distinction of the Trinity. For where the Son declared of himself, saying: I am the first and I am the last, he went on to add: And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit (Isa. 48). One in person, then, is the Lord the Father, another the Spirit of God the Father. And so, when the Son is read to be sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit, under the name of three persons the Holy Spirit is plainly shown to subsist of himself, just as in another place the same [prophet] distinguishes the proper being of the Trinity: Behold my servant, I will uphold him, my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased; I have put my Spirit upon him (Isa. 42). The Father calls his beloved servant, upon whom he has put his Spirit, to which Jesus Christ testifies with his own voice: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me (Luke 4). And so that this might be manifest also to the nations, Go, he says, baptise all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt., last chapter). There, under three persons, one work and one name assert an undivided majesty. We have, as has been said, according to Luke: And when Jesus had been baptised the heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: You are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased (Luke 3). The Son, then, is declared in the body, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, the Father in the voice. But in this place the dove is to be understood as a passing form, not an abiding substance.
CHAPTER VIII.
That it does not detract from the deity of the Holy Spirit that he appears to be neither begotten nor unbegotten.

But meanwhile, since we demonstrate the proper person of the Holy Spirit, and confess the Father unbegotten, and acknowledge the Son only-begotten, you ask me whether the Holy Spirit is to be confessed unbegotten, or begotten, or something else. The holy Scriptures speak of the power and deity of the Holy Spirit; whether he ought to be called begotten or unbegotten, they do not say. See what darkness of unbelief [such a man] makes for himself. You do not want to know what he did not wish to be unknown; and you want to know what he did not command to be inquired into. He did not say 'begotten', lest you believe him the Son; he did not say 'unbegotten', lest you think him the Father; but for the distinction of being he testified that he proceeds from the Father, as we read: The Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father. Since this is so, acknowledge at least in this way that the Holy Spirit has his own person. The difference of name proves that he is a third besides the two; the unity of majesty shows that he who proceeds from God is not third in order or rank. For he who comes forth from the inmost parts of God is proved to be not a creature of God but the substance of God. Do not scrutinise how he is God who is manifestly God. Here the reasoning is hidden; the truth is not hidden. Why ask how he is the partner and equal of the king, who is established to be of the king's honour and kind? And inquiry about a name is superfluous where there is no doubting about the loftiness. The Holy Spirit, then, proceeds from both; therefore he says: But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. And in another place: He breathed on [them] and said: Receive the Holy Spirit. You ask whether he is unbegotten or begotten. The sacred oracles have sung nothing about this; it is wrong to break the divine silences. What God did not think should be made known in his Scriptures, he did not wish you to make known or to know by superfluous curiosity. He made known that what pertains to your salvation ought to reach your conscience. What you should believe about the Holy Spirit, let us consult the holy oracles. For would you dare to say this very thing, that the Son is begotten, unless you had learned it from the heavenly testimony of the Scriptures? Or would you presume to assert that Christ the Lord was either born of the Virgin or begotten of a coeval and coeternal Father, had you not taken it from reading, had you not questioned the divine voices about God? And therefore, in order to know how you ought to agree concerning the Holy Spirit, you must return to the apostles and the Gospels, with whom and in whom you do not doubt that God has spoken. To return, then, to your needless proposition: does anything lie in this for the grace or the substance of the Holy Spirit, whether he be proved unbegotten or begotten? For it detracts nothing from the Son that he is not read to be unbegotten, nor from the Father that he is not held to be begotten. In expressions of this kind there is a propriety of designation, not a diversity of power or majesty. Begotten and unbegotten is a difference of person, not of nature. When, then, you have said or heard useless and unnecessary things about begotten and unbegotten, fit only for slanders, will you be content to stop at this point? Surely you will still ask whether he is God. When you have learned from what is read that he is true God, you will no longer have anything to ask, because once you have begun to know things strong and complete, you will not need to inquire into things empty and void. Where, then, the ground of usefulness and the fullness of truth are understood to be, there let a saving attention rest.
CHAPTER IX.
That the Holy Spirit is the perfecter and bestower of spiritual gifts.

That the Holy Spirit is the bestower of heavenly gifts and the dispenser of sanctifications, the very meaning of his name also declares. And his magnificence is manifest even in the Old Testament. For there his grace was granted only to certain chosen ones, that is, to the patriarchs and likewise the prophets, and to holy and elect men, so that through the very perfection of the gifts you may understand the dignity of the giver. And as far as is most manifestly found in the holy Scriptures, the Father works some things himself through himself, some specifically through the Son, some through the Holy Spirit, though under the prerogative of a common power. That we exist seems to be referred properly to the Father, in whom, as the Apostle says, we live, move and have our being. That we are capable of reason and wisdom and justice is assigned specifically to him who is reason and wisdom and justice, that is, to the Son. That being called we are regenerated, and being regenerated are renewed, and being renewed are sanctified, is plainly ascribed by the divine oracles to the person of the Holy Spirit. But the sacred pages speak thus under the distinction of the undivided Trinity, so that to anyone a diversity of work may appear in each, yet a unity of will remains in the three. So both pagans and catechumens share in the dispensation of the Father and the Son, but not readily in the sanctification and infusion of the Holy Spirit, unless they have already attained the most blessed [state], purified and made spiritual, and even apostolic, and prepared with all their spirit for martyrdom. And amid all this will he still be judged a creature by the impious, who within the undivided Trinity, in the ordering of human salvation, receives the more magnificent and more perfect gifts? But perhaps you say: The Holy Spirit is greater, whose works are greater and nobler. It is not so. For this is the custom of the Trinity: to whichever person it entrusts the office of administering a matter, to that person it ascribes the effect of the thing accomplished; so that though the work may perhaps be different, the purpose is common, and though there is a special act in each, a general counsel remains in the three; and therefore, though they have a distinct task in operation, they nevertheless hold one consent in the ordering. After the Lord's ascension, the Holy Spirit is described as having descended to heap up and fulfil his benefits; of him the Saviour himself speaks through John's Gospel: That Spirit of truth whom the Father will send in my name (John 14). The Father, he says, will send in my name — plainly of the Trinity. Of what creature have we ever read or heard it said that it came into this world in the name of God? This one, then, of whom Christ the Lord God says: Unless I go, the Paraclete will not come to you (John 16), is without doubt God, who is sent in the place of God to confirm the gifts of God. In these two sayings, under the distinction of the Trinity, the person of the Holy Spirit also is declared absolutely. Not without reason, therefore, is this too referred to the equality of Godhead, that just as the Son, so also the Holy Spirit is called Paraclete in the Scriptures. And how shall we be able to prove this? Certainly from the authority of the apostle John, when he says: If any of us, he says, has sinned, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2). Paraclete, that is, advocate, which refers to the person of the Son, or also comforter, which pertains to the Holy Spirit: the one Greek word signifies both. In John's Gospel we have: And I, he says, will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete (John 14). Another Paraclete, that is, of like power, of the Father's glory, of the same nature. And another Paraclete: if you think the Holy Spirit is one of the creatures, it is unworthy that a creature, descending, should confirm the same benefits that the Creator conferred, and that, as if the power of the maker had been ineffective, the completion of the finished work should be reserved for a creature, however excellent, but only a creature. You, then, revile with the reproach of 'creature' the Holy Spirit, to whom the Son of God made himself equal by divine testimony and his own utterance. And another Paraclete: here you will recognise a twofold sense and a distinction of person. [You say that] Christ seems to have made himself equal, under the name of Paraclete, to the Holy Spirit, who is in fact the material and handiwork of God's work, because Jesus himself is proved to have been created from Mary; for this unbelieving word the argument is very weak. For if you think Christ was likened to the Paraclete according to [his] humanity, not even this fits the truth. For he was made a little lower than the angels, and became one of us; he could not well be compared to the first and heavenly, and, as you assert, more excellent creature. But if Christ said this according to the form of God, it is certain that the maker ought not to have been compared with the thing made. And if as man he makes himself equal to this more excellent creature, it is pride in the lesser; if as God, it is an insult to the greater. Since, then, this comparison is not recognised to hold good within the condition of a creature, it remains that both be believed to be God, and that an equality of divinity be compared between them mutually. For when the Saviour speaks through John: And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive (ibid.), he who can be given to the whole world is manifestly the God of the world. Here too recognise the threefold power: the Father is the one indicated as to be asked, the Son the one understood as going to ask, the Holy Spirit the one promised as to be sent by the Father. Observe that the person of the Holy Spirit is not associated, as you assert, with kindred creatures, but is joined in all things to the Trinity in works and made equal in powers.
CHAPTER X.
The assertion of the Trinity is repeated from the Acts of the Apostles, where Christ is also asserted, against the Novatians, to have been sent to grant repentance.

In the Acts of the Apostles Peter, discoursing about the Lord Jesus Christ, speaks thus: Being therefore exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which you see and hear (Acts 2). In the right hand the Son is designated, in God the Father, and in the proper sense of his own name the Holy Spirit. And in what follows we read: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, by him this man stands before you whole (Acts 4). Observe here too the distinction of the Trinity expressed: Peter, bearing the Holy Spirit within himself, speaks of the Son dying in the flesh and of the Father raising him, and the apostolic [text] repeats it nonetheless: They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and spoke the word of God with confidence (Acts 2). Notice in this place also that the Holy Spirit is contained in the Trinity. In the prayer let the Father, who is asked, be recognised; in the word of God, the Son; in the steadfastness of the apostles the Spirit, the fire, is at work. They were all, it says, filled with the Holy Spirit. It belongs to manifest majesty to be able to pour itself into very many at once by the subtlety of incorporeal divinity, and to remain whole without loss. Again, when the apostles had said of Jesus: Him God has exalted with his right hand as prince and saviour, to grant repentance to Israel for the remission of sins, We, they say, are witnesses of these things, and [so is] the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to all who obey him (Acts 5). Understand here that, within the order of the Trinity, the Son is appointed by the Father not only to preach but to grant repentance, and that the Holy Spirit is poured into those who comply, to reward their obedience. Stephen, at the moment of his passion, is filled with the Holy Spirit, and, the gates of righteousness being unbarred, the Son is revealed at the right hand of the Father, as he himself, filled with the Holy Spirit, declares: Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing at the right hand of God. See how he performed the offices of his passion in sight of the Trinity. Peter addresses Cornelius the centurion, saying: Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit. God anointed, that is, power filled [him], blessing poured into [him], divinity penetrated [him]. How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit: these three evidently show their own properties: the gift, the giver, the one gifted; the anointer, the anointed, the ointment; as the divine word says in another place: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness. In the humanity taken up God is anointed, and God anoints, and in the descent of the heavenly dove the power of the Father is recognised; it is not lawful that this Holy Spirit, by whom Christ the Son of man, already full of the Son of God, is filled, should be believed to be anything other than God. For if he were a creature, how could he penetrate the incorporeal nature that penetrates all things? For the Trinity holds itself, as [it is said]: I in the Father and the Father in me (John 14). And again: The Spirit searches even the deep things of God (1 Cor. 2). Again: The Spirit who proceeds from the Father (John 15). Unless this Spirit were from the Father, and dwelt by nature infused in the Father's eternity, he could not proceed from the Father. But you ask whether the Spirit always proceeds from the Father: always with him, always from him; as heat from fire, so he is brought forth without interruption, so that he knows how to go out but does not know how to be separated. For if the procession of the Holy Spirit were not everlasting, his substance would seem to be local; if one does not penetrate the other without mingling, by the incorporeal union of their brightness, the divinity will be confused. For mingling removes the distinctness of the threefold essence, whereas mutual infusion shows a distinct essence, which can be seen to lie midway between substance and persons. To substance belongs that which subsists; to the persons belongs that each subsists properly for itself. Paul addresses his disciples, saying: I do not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to rule the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood. How clearly the whole Trinity is designated in its persons! He declares the counsel of God the Father; he affirms that the bishops were ordained by the Holy Spirit; he shows also that Christ, by whose blood the Church was purchased, is God. To the Romans too the Trinity is set out under the proper sense of the names: But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you (Rom. 8). The Father raises, the Son is raised, and because of the indwelling Spirit life is promised to mortal bodies that are to be raised again. And in what follows: But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. When he says the Spirit of God, and in what follows the Spirit of Christ, notice that here he designates the person of Christ under the name of God. Or if here he signifies under the name of God the Father, whose Spirit he is, see, here the Holy Spirit is declared through unity of substance to be the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son, and is rightly recognised to proceed from both, and is seen to have a distinct person within the bond of the Trinity, and he who does not have the Holy Spirit is shown not to have Christ either. The Holy Spirit is therefore God, and when he is denied, Christ too is denied, who said: No one comes to the Father except through me. He who is empty of the Holy Spirit is not Christ's, and loses the way by which one reaches the Father.
CHAPTER XI.
That it is proper to God to sanctify the creature.

The First Epistle to the Corinthians: And such indeed you were, but you have been washed, but you have been justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God (1 Cor. 6). See, here too, with mention of our God, that is, of the Father, the Holy Spirit sanctifies the faithful of Corinth with Christ working together. No creature can at all sanctify another. The bestowal of sanctification is the munificence of majesty alone. In this place, in the name of Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God, recognise three persons. In the Second to the Corinthians: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be always with you all (2 Cor., last ch.). The grace of Christ, the love of God, the communion of the Holy Spirit: he has evidently expressed three persons. Again in the Second to the Corinthians: But he who confirms us with you in Christ, and who has anointed us, is God, who has also sealed us and given us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts (2 Cor. 1). Hence he confirms the unity of the undivided Trinity in its works, and he seals us properly through Christ, and, being about to give himself, he gives already in the present the Holy Spirit as pledge. In earthly business the amount of the earnest is some portion of the contract on behalf of which it has been given, but the nature of a pledge exceeds the value of the thing for which it is seen to be laid down. Here, however, since the pledge does not know how to be preferred to the majesty, it must be made equal to it. For perfect things cannot be surpassed. The Father, therefore, grants the pledge of the Holy Spirit in place of himself. So let nothing in the Holy Spirit be thought half-full or over-full; let him be thought full, because he is compared to fullness. For it is not lawful that he who is given in God's stead by way of pledge should be believed to be anything other than God. Again to Titus: He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ (Titus 3). See, here too, within the Trinity, the Father manifestly pours out the abundance of the Holy Spirit through the Son. And what is especially to be noticed, he ascribes the power of regeneration and renewal to the Holy Spirit himself. Peter also in his Epistle sets out the unconquerable Trinity in its persons, saying: According to the foreknowledge of God the Father and the sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, grace and peace be multiplied to you (1 Pet. 1). In the foreknowledge the Father, and in the sanctification the Spirit, in the sprinkling of blood Christ is shown.
CHAPTER XII.
That the Holy Spirit is not local.

Let us demonstrate the Holy Spirit to be God from his powers and works. Every creature, as it is subject to beginnings in time, so is known to be local, circumscribed by fixed spaces and bounds. The Holy Spirit is enclosed by no limits as a thing made is; he must be held to be God, by reason of the very freedom of his diffused majesty. The word of the Lord Saviour to the apostles is: The Father, he says, will give you the Spirit of truth, to be with you for ever. If he is local, and remained in them perpetually, he certainly could not be elsewhere. Let us see whether his nature is to be bounded by local limits. The Lord says to the apostles: You will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth (Acts 1). After his ascension the Holy Spirit came upon them, and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. Let us see why the blessings of diverse tongues are given first: surely so that they might be made fit for the instruction of the peoples of the faithful. And that he is recorded to have sat upon each one, the reason is that he may be understood not to have been divided among many, but to have remained whole in each; but as is the way of waxen fires (for, as we know, kindled fire has this nature, that to as many as look upon it, upon the tresses of its purple brightness, it imparts the use of its light, to so many it grants the service of its gift, and nonetheless remains in its own wholeness), so the power of the Holy Spirit, however much it flows out, however much the grace of divine bounty overflows into very many, just as it is proved to admit no measure, so it has felt no expenditure. Recognise God from the dignity of the works. The apostles, full of the Holy Spirit, about to dispense the treasures of salvation through the whole world, carry this heavenly gift about in themselves and transfer it to others by the laying on of hands. It is given to the receivers without loss to the giver. He is handed over whole to believers, and is possessed whole by those who hand him over; by his infusion the whole world is filled; he is spread without being thinned, dispersed without division. Especially on that most holy night of regeneration, from East to West, from the rising of the sun to its setting, from the north and the sea, everywhere the same Spirit, one and full, is at work; he is present through all things, believed in by invocation, felt by blessing; countless multitudes are washed in one baptism and, as the Apostle said, are made to drink of one Spirit, and are reborn into the bosom of one adopting [Father]. And therefore God said: In those days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. Notice that he said: I will pour out of my Spirit, and did not say: I will pour out my Spirit, that is, as much of him as the world could receive by dispensation. You see that he goes forth from the Father yet is not separated from the Father; he is sent out and not lost; he is poured out and retained; and in that he is read to be poured out, the greatness of his fullness is declared. The book of Genesis testifies at the beginning of the sacred volume: And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters; was borne, it says, over the waters (Gen. 1): the word itself seems to assign [to him] the abundance of one who fills all things and the eminence of one who rules. This proper magnificence of his too, circumscribed by no spaces of place, [Scripture] celebrates with like testimony, saying: Where shall I go from your spirit? (Ps. 138), that is, where shall I hide myself from the sight of him who I do not doubt is present through all things, that is, within and without; whose eye, penetrating the abysses, I dread within the secrets of my breast; to whose presence I know that all things he made are subject? Understand clearly that it was said of him, since he is a consuming fire: Nor is there anyone who hides himself from his heat (Ps. 18). His ineffable greatness enters, fills and exceeds the depths of the underworld, the expanse of the waves, the extent of the lands, the heights of the heavens. He is said to be sent by the Father and the Son, and to proceed from their substance, and is recognised to do one work with them; and therefore the Son says of him: The Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father (John 15). He did not say who was created by the Father, but proceeds from the Father, that is, from the fellowship of the Father's power and from the property of his nature. But from the very word, since he is said to proceed from the Father, it is shown that he has no beginning, [being] with the Father. What is it, then, that the Son is said to be born of God the Father, and the Holy Spirit is signified to proceed? If you ask what difference there is between one being born and one proceeding, the difference is evidently this: that the one is born of one, the other goes forth from both. Since, then, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, he shows three privileges of deity in himself: that he is proved to subsist in his own person, to endure without any space of time, and to exist wholly from the substance of the Father. When, therefore, he is said to proceed, by the very property of the word he is recognised to be circumscribed by no laws of time, but to lack beginning and end. And since we read: I am who am, and, He who is has sent me (Exod. 3), proceeds likewise indicates the same. For to be and to proceed are the expression of one eternity. So the procession itself, touching neither first nor last, is understood to be subject to no beginning or end. We do not, then, believe him to be local because we have learned from reading that he is sent by the Father; for of the Father and the Son too we read that they descend and come as if by some movement. Let us see where. I, he says, and the Father will come, and make our dwelling with him (John 14). And again, when the giants were striving to raise a tower to heaven, the person of the Father speaks: Come, and let us confuse their tongues (Gen. 11). Here, then, through the sounds of our words the effecting of things is shown to our senses. But divine power does not admit local motion; it neither arrives by an advancing course nor departs by a gliding return. Since it exceeds all things, where would it withdraw to? Of the Holy Spirit we have learned from reading: And the Church had peace throughout all Judaea, walking in the fear of the Lord, and was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit (Acts 9). And how, amid these things, does anyone presume to assert that he is a local creature, who is proved to fill the Church of an infinite multitude, so that it is plain that what the Apostle says also belongs to him: The Father of mercies and God of all consolation (2 Cor. 1)? We have in the psalm: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God (Ps. 45). What is this rush of the river, if not surely that of which the Lord speaks through John: He who believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly? This the Lord Jesus said of the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive (John 7). See the magnificence of the majesty. He is so given on earth to the Church of God that he yet gladdens in heaven the city of God, that is, the citizens of the heavenly kingdoms, the peoples of the heavenly host, principalities, powers and dominions: he waters them with ineffable joys in the awareness of eternal blessedness, and inebriates them more overflowingly with the abundance of gladness, and rouses the concert of heaven to exultation by the torrent of his sanctification. If you suppose that such great things are given through some creature, you leave nothing proper to divine power. If, I say, you reckon these things [given] through some creature, you go on to insult the angels and archangels, to whom you reckon such great things to be bestowed by the largess of a fellow servant.
BOOK TWO.
CHAPTER ONE.
That no rational creature can be poured into a kindred creature.

We read of the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit: But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. Who, then, except one who was of the same fullness, could fill him who fills all things? Of the apostles the divine word reports: And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with confidence. And a little later: How he is said to fill even whole nations, and yet is recognised to remain inexhaustible and full in himself. If the Spirit is created, of what angel or archangel has it ever been read that, received inwardly, he poured himself into any soul? Tell me, if you have ever read of any power and might among creatures that fills and possesses many things at once and, what is more, remains undiminished and [un]divided. It is impossible that a spiritual and rational creature should ever be able to be poured into a nature kindred to itself. So too a material thing cannot penetrate a material substance. God alone, in whom the Holy Spirit also is understood, simple, subtle, pure, glides into his handiwork, whether angelic or human, by the power of incorporeal divinity, which alone penetrates its own work and enters the hidden places of the human heart. But no heavenly creature can so far pour itself into or fill a man as to be able to know the hidden things of human thought. And therefore we read of God alone: You who alone know the hearts of men (Prov. 6). And again: For it knows how to discern hidden things. And if this is proper to divinity, how much more is it a mark of majesty to search the depths of the most high God in the person of the Holy Spirit. This privilege is owed to the Author alone, that he can enter the secret conscience. A soul can be joined to a soul, or an angel to an angel, but cannot be poured into it, because creatures of this kind are capable only of the Holy Spirit, that is, of God alone; because they are the vessels of their potter, they can be filled only by him by whom they were made from nothing, and without whom they are felt to be empty. So the substance of the soul, being corporeal matter, cannot at all be poured into another rational creature. For compared with the grossness of the outer man the soul can be called incorporeal, but referred to its author, to whom its matter is comprehensible and his handiwork palpable, by whom it can be enclosed and bound within a body and consigned to everlasting fire, as we read: that they may go into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels; to this author it is undoubtedly something corporeal. But perhaps you say: It is plain that even the troublesome violence of demons frequently pours itself into men whom it has received to tempt. It is not so: for they can enter the recesses of the body, but cannot reach the inner parts of the soul. It must be known, then, that the deceitful subtlety of spiritual wickedness disturbs by its onset those parts of the limbs which are at times wearied by too much wine or by the heat of fever. Thus hostile temptation knows how to creep into the senses of the soul through malice, but cannot flow into the recesses of the soul by nature. And therefore human minds and breasts take in such unclean spirits not by an infusion of natures, but conceive them by depravity of will. It is plain, therefore, that they cannot penetrate the substances of souls whose consciences they cannot know. And if it ever happens that demons know [them], it comes from a ruinous complicity, not from the power of nature. Divine power alone, then, which is also in the Holy Spirit, mingles itself with rational creatures, poured into them and poured around them, as in a special way it rested with overflowing grace in that body of the Lord's manhood taken from his mother Mary, as the Son says of himself: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me (Luke 4). If, then, the Holy Spirit were a thing made, of subject condition, as they say, it would have been as impossible as it was unworthy of God that any creature should fill the soul or body in which the Son of God, that is God, already was, in which, as the Apostle says, the fullness of the Godhead already dwelt bodily (Col. 2). If the Holy Spirit is a creature, how can corruption possess the incorruptible, and a frail condition possess one capable of majesty? If the Holy Spirit is one of the common crowd of made creatures, how is a creature presumed to be made equal, as it were, with the creator, that is, with the Son of God, and a servant to share one lodging with the Lord in the soul of the Saviour, and, as though the presence of the author were not sufficient in him, a servant comes to add to the heap of holiness? It is not so. Rather, the heavenly fellowship recognises the temple as shared with itself. Nor is it surprising if in that illustrious soul of the blessed body the Son and the Holy Spirit share one dwelling, to whom heaven too is evidently common.
CHAPTER II.
Whether, according to the opinion of the unlearned, the Holy Spirit was incarnate like the Son, since he too came upon Mary; or whether the Son alone was begotten of the Virgin.

But it is said: If the Holy Spirit dwelt in the body and soul of the Redeemer, then the Spirit too will seem to have taken on incarnation. It is not so. For before the beginnings of the creation Mary's body is filled by the Holy Spirit, and at the beginnings of the creation the Son of the Virgin is conceived with the Holy Spirit cooperating, but [the body] was to be possessed specially by the person of the Son for nine months, and coming forth into the light with him [the Spirit] is poured in; the person of the Holy Spirit certainly does not take on the fellowship of that time within the secret of the virginal womb. So the man whom the Son of God takes up at the very beginnings, the Holy Spirit entered not as one who takes [him] up but as sanctifier. For the one is born, the other is poured in. Of the Son of the Virgin it can be said personally and specially that he is the soul or flesh of the Son of God, but the Holy Spirit can in no way be called soul or flesh. Whereas the Son of God is therefore called the God of glory crucified in him, it can in no way be said that the Holy Spirit suffered in him. So there is a diversity of works, not a diversity of substances. For just as we cannot say that the Father descended in the form of a dove, or that the Son spoke in the Father's voice when he said: This is my Son (Matt. 3), so you cannot assert that the Holy Spirit was born of the Virgin, or lived specially in the flesh of the Redeemer, or was crucified in his passion, or was restored to the body in the resurrection, or was raised up to heaven in the ascension. These things must necessarily be assigned to the work and person of the Son, but it is not fitting to ascribe them to the Holy Spirit, though the unity of will is kept intact. Meanwhile Macedonius asserts that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Let him begin where he sees fit, provided he presumes to do nothing with his own words and does not go beyond the sacred pages in disputing, but brings forward, if he can, authority from testimonies throughout, which may prevail in both number and force against the faith of the whole world. Without doubt great allegations and copious and very evident proofs are needed for anyone to prove that he is one of the number of creatures whom all the kingdoms of the earth celebrate together as of the same honour and glory with the Father and the Son; whom the Catholic Church, regenerated in him, acknowledges as her creator. And rightly she does not hesitate to believe him [her] author whom she perceives as [her] restorer.
CHAPTER III.
The objection of Macedonius, by which he impiously asserts that the Holy Spirit is a more excellent creature.

I call him a creature, he says, but more excellent than all creatures. We said beforehand that we would rest our case not on our own persuasions but on Catholic oracles. Since, then, we are treating of God, let prophet, apostle and evangelist answer. You call him a creature more excellent than all creatures. Show in which books you have read these words about the Holy Spirit. Not, I think, in the Old; you will not show [it] in the New? Since, then, you cannot produce [it], while you fail to make your case we confirm ours. While you do not prove him a creature, even with us silent you show him to be creator. So, since this assertion of yours does not belong to the Catholic sense, nor at all to Christian teaching, recognise the devil's invention, who, wherever he sees the house of the soul empty of the Holy Spirit, invades it with the hostile guests, as it were, of sevenfold wickedness. For whoever shuts the one out takes the other in. This more excellent creature was in him who, shining forth in heavenly splendour, aware of his gift, ignorant of his author, saw that he had, but did not know that he had received; and therefore the glory which he did not understand when blessed, he lost when proud, saying thus: I will ascend above the stars of the clouds, I will set my seat upon the throne, and I will be like the Most High. He, then, as I suppose, had no one among creatures above himself, saw no one between himself and God, in rivalry with whom he might rise up, roused by the goad of pride; and therefore, seeing no one standing before him in the order of the heavenly host, he presumed to make himself equal to the very Lord of things. But if, impatient of a greater, he had found anyone more excellent than himself in heavenly joy, he would rather have tried to compare or prefer himself to that one. There are two [kinds] in heaven: he who rules, and those who are ruled; no third kind has existed between these, which would be greater than the second and lower than the highest. You can perhaps say 'more excellent creature' of the archangels, though they surpass the rest more in rank than in nature. But the archangels too serve the Holy Spirit, one of whom, as a minister, announced his coming to blessed Mary. But you say: See where the prophet Amos clearly assigns the Holy Spirit to be a creature, saying thus: Behold, I who make firm the thunder and create the spirit (Amos 4). First, the name 'spirit' sometimes can by no means be referred to the person of the sanctifying Spirit unless you add either 'Spirit of God', or 'Holy Spirit', or 'the Spirit blows where it wills', that is, unless you add the dignity either of his work or of his proper name. Next, if you look to the order of the reading, he has shown this creature, more excellent as you assert, to be too much despised. For he described it as a creature after the thunder. Hence it would have been inconsistent that, by your sense, he should place this chief work of God after an irrational element, or pair it with one. I do not say of the person of an angel, but of any just man, it would be unworthy to believe this. Let us think it closer and friendlier to reason, then, if after the thunder we understand the blasts of winds to be signified, as in that [verse] in the psalms: Spirit of storms, which perform his word (Ps. 148), or that: Sulphur, spirit of storms (Ps. 10), or: With a vehement spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish (Ps. 47). Spirit is understood in diverse ways when it is not specially designated with its privileges. But leaving these aside, consult the truth of the Hebrew translation, and there you will detect the shameful error of your persuasion. For you will find it said there thus: For behold, I who form the mountains and create the wind. See how bare and how empty were the words against God that you believed. See with how great an argument you armed yourself against the power of the majesty; and after this you do not fear to cling to so weak a twig, you who hang over so dreadful a precipice.
CHAPTER IV.
Macedonius, asserting a duality, denies that the Holy Spirit has a person of his own.

Next you bring in a duality, and say that the Holy Spirit does not have a person of his own; nor do you perceive that you have lost the grace of regeneration, you who strive to offend [against] regeneration, [against him] whom divine truth declares to be united with [Father and Son] in common majesty and power, saying thus: Go, it says, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. In the name, it says, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. last ch.). The singularity of the name speaks of unity, the diversity of the designations of Trinity. In name, then, one; but in the distinction of persons, not one. What is the prerogative of a single name in three, if not the undivided concord of the deity? Make a step [of rank] if you can, where, by God's own testimony, you find nothing but one. You hear three, so that the impiety of Sabellius may not mingle and confuse the unity. You hear one, so that the perversity of Arius may not divide the Trinity. You hear Holy Spirit, so that the express property of a distinct name may pierce Macedonius through. And so it is the unchangeable work not of a creature but of the Creator that is performed where the abolition of sins and immunity are bestowed. Yet in this indivisible embrace of majesty, in the property of person the Father is one, the Son is another, the Holy Spirit is another, but in unity [they are] not another thing. Certainly, if he were not God, he could not have a person of his own beside the Father and the Son. Indeed, when the Word passes into flesh, and God puts on the condition of man, and [sets] round about himself his tabernacle, and wraps his splendour in the darkness of our frailty, and makes darkness his hiding-place, there is indeed a twofold substance of God and man, but nevertheless one person. Why so? Because when God, taking the form of a servant, is joined to the servant, the lowliness of the lesser is hidden within the dignity of the greater, and is consumed by the light of the higher which emptied itself, and so the humanity, with the divinity overshadowing or surpassing it, does not obtain the property of a person. There, then, can there be parity of persons where equality of merits and dignities exists. And therefore you should know that the Holy Spirit possesses with the Father and the Son the one privilege of majesty, since you see that he holds the proper right of a person. But if someone should object and say: If in Christ, God and man alike, we speak of two substances, why should we not by similar reasoning believe two persons? It is not so. For whoever makes two persons in Christ introduces the impiety of a quaternity, which the nature of things utterly does not admit. Out of two rational and diverse substances, especially of God and man, of Creator and creature, one cannot be made; but out of two persons one can be made, as we read that the head and the body, Christ and the Church, hold one person. For, it says, the two shall be in one flesh. And just as among us men the son of the head of a household beside his father, or a slave beside his master, does not have the standing of a person of his own, so in God and man there is indeed a twin substance, but not a twin person, because a person can consume a person, but a substance cannot consume a substance. For a person is a matter of law, a substance a matter of nature. At this point it seems necessary that we establish by testimonies one person and two substances in Christ, Lord and man alike. Give [proof of] the one person of the Redeemer, God and man. The Apostle says: For if they had known the wisdom of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. If you ask how the inviolable could suffer and the incomprehensible be crucified, the unity of the person brings it about that what the man endured, God is believed to have endured. Likewise when the evangelist records: No one ascends except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven: how does he here speak of the Son of Man before the day of the passion, or of the resurrection or of the ascension, and assert that he descended from heaven and remains in the heavens, unless the reasoning of truth resolves this through the unity of the person? So in another place the person of head and body is joined, when one reads: For I was hungry and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me to drink. What does the unity of the person say? The man is fed and God is refreshed. The foot is tended and the head testifies that it feels the soothing. He says, then: They would never have crucified the Lord of glory. And conversely: No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. See how through the unity of the person human things are mingled with divine and divine with human. God is crucified, and the man is said to descend from heaven and to remain in heaven. This being so, let us examine from the sacred volumes the distinction of the twin substance. Blessed Moses says: You shall eat the head with the feet, and you shall devour its entrails (Exod. 12). In the feet let us believe [there is] the humanity, and in the head the majesty. So it comes about that, while by searching faith we recognise these things lying hidden within the letter, we consume the entrails, that is, the hidden things of the mysteries. For the eagerness to devour is understood as zeal for searching. So also in another place the same revealer of the sacraments hints at the resolution of the twofold substance, saying: Foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8, Luke 9). That is: deceitful heresies and dark or airy powers have set their seat in human breasts in deep damnation, but [I have no place] in the hearts of the faithful who see the man in the flesh and do not believe that God lies hidden within the man; for holes and nests signify not passing and momentary dwellings, but ones founded in lasting and secure possession, which multiply the serpentine nourishment of vices. For the Apostle, setting aside the obscurity of the sacrament, plainly added the two substances, saying thus: The fathers, of whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. But you say: the Apostle in the volume of his works acknowledges only two persons, as he says to the Corinthians: Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God. And to the Galatians: Paul an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead. And again: one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him. On these grounds you say no mention is made of the Holy Spirit. To put it briefly, you have forgotten that the Apostle, full of the Holy Spirit, preached these things about the Father and the Son with that very Spirit inspiring the apostles. So to him who spoke of the working of the Father and the Son, he too was not absent who dictated what was to be spoken, according to this: No one says Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit. You see, then, that whoever is going to believe or confess or preach Christ will first have the Holy Spirit in himself. Do not, then, burden your faith because the Father and the Son are sometimes mentioned without mention of the Holy Spirit. For often, with the Father's name suppressed, the working of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is preached. Saint Ananias says to Paul: Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you were coming, has sent me, that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Here there is plainly a connection of two persons. See, Paul is rebuked [and] blinded by Christ, is filled [and] enlightened by the Holy Spirit, and no mention of the Father is inserted here. Likewise when Paul asked certain of the disciples, Into what were you baptized? — who, it was clear, had been baptized in the baptism of John after the Lord's ascension — after the baptism of the Trinity had been preached, since that mystery too by which John had been accustomed to baptize, that is, into him who is to come, was shown to have been omitted in their baptism, as Paul the apostle said: John indeed baptized, but into him who is to come (Acts 19), that is to say: you were not baptized thus. When Paul asked them: Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? — [those] who, after the baptism of the Saviour, would properly have been [completed] through the laying on of hands — they confess [it]. And they answered: We have not even heard whether there is a spirit. On hearing this they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. Note that when they are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, they afterwards receive the Holy Spirit, and prophetic power from the invocation of the Paraclete. Truly he is God who after God's gift is not read [...], but only, as must be believed, with the Son [...]. When the Holy Spirit had come upon them, then they spoke in tongues and prophesied. See how great is the power of the Holy Spirit. In baptism the remission of sins is granted; at the coming of the Holy Spirit the gifts of powers are conferred, and by the confirmed the miracles of signs are performed. For those estranged from the truth are accustomed to cavil even about syllables. For although we know it was said absolutely of the Trinity, that from him and through him and in him are all things (Rom. 8), they assert that 'from him' is more than 'through him', and again that this preposition, that is 'through', is of greater prerogative than 'in him'. But if they think 'in him' is said of the Holy Spirit with a diminution of power, let them hear the magnificence of this preposition, and accept that even by their own assertion it is to be understood of the Holy Spirit. In him, it says, we live, move, and are (Acts 17). And rightly do we live, move and are in him in whom we have been restored and regenerated. But we recognise that 'through him' too is to be referred to the Holy Spirit, as you have [it]: To one through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge (1 Cor. 12). Likewise to the Hebrews: Who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God. And again: The love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy [Spirit] himself, who has been given to us. And if we understand [it] also of the Father, we find 'from him' said likewise of the Holy Spirit. As we have in the Gospel of John: What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit (John 3). And at the close of the chapter: So is everyone who is born of the Spirit. Thus, then, it does not prejudice the Holy Spirit when, with his name suppressed, the works of the Father and the Son are recorded, just as the Father and the Son are not denied when the work and power of the Holy Spirit are specially affirmed, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence (Acts 1). So also in the Gospel it is stated of the single person of the Holy Spirit: Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God (John 3). Are the Father and the Son, because they are not named in this place, to be believed absent from so great and so divine a gift? It is not so. For without doubt, since they are joined in mysteries and benefits to the Holy Spirit, with whom they have one substance, they are present, if not by mention, yet by the unity of goodness and of work.
CHAPTER V.
The objection that the saying we read, Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, testifies that water and the Holy Spirit alike are a creature.

But you say: The Holy Spirit is a creature to such a degree that he is seen to be joined to the element of water, which is placed here in the first position and order, according to the Gospel saying recalled above: Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God (ibid.). For it is plain that whoever says this is ignorant not only of the divine power in the Holy Spirit, but of the very rationale of baptism [...] with Christ (Rom. 6). But if you ask how we can die or rise with Christ, take note. All of us who are immersed in the sacred font imitate the death and burial of the Redeemer, as the same Apostle says: Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ have been baptized into his death? For we have been buried with him through baptism into death (Rom. 6). For just as he was laid in the tomb by a death of three days, so we too, laid down within the water, that is, within the substance of a kindred creature, by a threefold immersion, are buried as we go down and are raised as we come up. So through the water the imitation of burial is celebrated; through the Holy Spirit the reality of life and the hope of eternal salvation are conferred. Lastly, let the invocation of the Holy Spirit be removed, and let us see whether the pouring of that water alone can be of any benefit. So it is a creature that performs the office of burying; it is God who grants the benefit of being reborn. Him, then, whom you perceive to be the parent of renewal, acknowledge to be also the author of resurrection. Of him the prophet prophesies, and speaks thus to the Father: Send forth [your] Spirit and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth (Ps. 103). What is the difference between the working of the water and that of the Holy Spirit? Through the water we are seen to be led down into the tomb; through the Holy Spirit we are seen to be prepared for the kingdom.
CHAPTER VI.
Where it is asked whether the title Holy Spirit is to be thought a surname or a name.

But amid these things you think it must be asked whether the title of the Holy Spirit, who must necessarily be called God, is a name or perhaps a surname. But I recognise that what we are accustomed among men to add to a name does not befit the majesty of God; whatever is in his name is in no way adjectival, but without doubt eternal by nature. Even grammatical teaching calls some nouns common, that is, appellative, and names others specific, that is, proper. Let us see whether we can find something similar in our [matters] at this point. Grant in God a specific or proper name, that is, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. These are proper to such a degree that neither can the Father be said of the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit readily read of the Father. Likewise grant a proper [name]: unbegotten, proceeding from both. Again grant a general and common name: majesty, immensity, fullness, one, alone, God. But when you hear one, number does not begin here, but infinite perfection is gathered together. What is one, if not an incommunicable name, which admits neither a later nor an earlier? What is one, if not a simple, uncompounded and undivided substance? What is one, if not incommunicable and without equal, and always the same, who could never be different from himself? And so the common title [expresses] unity. When, then, you have said Father, Son and Holy Spirit, you have set out the persons of each alike. When you have said one God, you have shown the common substance of the Trinity, the common glory. Here, then, lack of skill has drawn over itself the night of error, when, suppressing the term of majesty, it judges the Holy Spirit only by that name which, as we said, is proper to him, rather than by what he has in common with the Father and the Son.
CHAPTER VII.
That the Holy Spirit specifically fills the prophets, and is equally to be believed and called God, is proved by clear testimonies.

Since the Holy Spirit is related to have spoken specifically through Moses and David and Isaiah, or other prophets, the divine words declare that God spoke, as is frequent in the volume of the Pentateuch: The Lord spoke, it says, to Moses, saying.
