Let us inquire more carefully whether the Holy Spirit specifically speaks in the prophets. We have, as we said before, in the Acts of the Apostles, when Paul is reproving the Jews: Well, he says, did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah to our fathers: Hearing you will hear, and you will not understand (Acts, last ch.). And in the same reading: Men, brothers, the scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David (Acts 1). And in the epistle of Peter we read: For prophecy was never brought by human will, but the holy men of God spoke by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet. 1). Let us recognise that prophetic grace plainly belongs to the power of the Holy Spirit. And of the psalm of David we read thus to the Hebrews: Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today, if you hear his voice (Ps. 94). And here too he most openly testifies that the Holy Spirit spoke through David. But let us see whether he is God, through whom all prophecy is recorded as inspired. Luke asserts that it is the Lord God who spoke through the prophets, saying thus: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and wrought the redemption of his people. And he added: As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old. Absolutely, the Holy Spirit, who had inspired the prophets, is proclaimed by the Gospel oracle to be the Lord and God of Israel. And in what follows, Simeon, full of the Holy Spirit: He had received, it says, an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless he first saw the Christ of the Lord (Luke 2). When he had seen him and taken him up in his arms in an embrace, he blessed God, that is, him from whom he was seen to have received the answer. He blessed God and said: Now, Lord, you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word. And absolutely he calls the Holy Spirit Lord God, by whose word and answer he had received that he would see Christ. You see that it must be understood specifically of the Holy Spirit when it is said in the prophets: The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken; I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me (Ps. 49). Here this name, that is, of the Lord, by whose word and answer he had received that he would see Christ, you see must be understood specifically of the Holy Spirit, when we are told in the prophets: The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken. And: I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me. Here you should know that this name, that is, Lord God, is to be referred to the person of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in David; or at least, in the one God acknowledge the will of the three, the power of the three, the substance of the three; for when you have said Father, one person is understood; when you have said God, the whole Trinity is designated. We also learn in the Acts of the Apostles that he who foretold the sufferings of Christ through the prophets is undoubtedly God, when it says: But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has thus fulfilled his Christ (Acts 3); that is, [Christ] imbued with the spiritual gift of his anointing. And again: As God spoke through the mouth of his holy ones (Luke 1). His holy ones, because sanctification belongs properly to the Holy Spirit. We read in Jeremiah: Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord (Jer. 23)? Who is this Lord who says through Jeremiah that he fills heaven and earth, if not the Holy Spirit, who also filled Jeremiah himself with prophetic power and the spirit of truth? If, then, [as] through the prophetic dispensation, so also the grace of the second birth the will of the Trinity assigns above all to the Holy Spirit, as he says in John: What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. And in another place the power of renewing man is written to lie with the Holy Spirit: But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence (John 3). And as was said above: Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit. And to Titus: He saved us, it says, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Let us see who this is whose sons we are made through the grace of adoption. He gave them, it says, power to become sons of God. And again: Who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God. You see most plainly that this Holy Spirit in whom we are reborn is God, with whose fatherhood we are endowed. He himself assigns this in another place more clearly than light: I will be to them a father, it says, and they will be to me sons and daughters, says the Lord almighty (Tit. 1). Rightly almighty, who blots out the bond of sin, who loosens the chains of consciences, and strips the man who believes in him of the foulness of corrupted nature, and adorns him with the garment of innocence, the beauty of justice, the robe of immortality, and enrols his sons in the angelic state by loving fatherhood. Let no one think the Holy Spirit is to be classed with creatures. He is outside the condition of servitude who can grant eternal freedom. For, says the Apostle, you did not receive the spirit of servitude again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, and the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God (Rom. 8). Undoubtedly he is God who makes sons of God through the remission of sins. It is agreed that the whole creation, even of angels and archangels, was liable to sin; yet their obedience, diligence and love toward God the fall of the transgressors established; the humility of submission became the confirmation of stability, the recognition of frailty, the Holy Spirit. Unless he were free above all, he could not make free men out of slaves. For if he were a creature, however much he conferred the grace of holiness, the consciousness of a debtor would still have remained. And therefore it says: No one can forgive sins but God alone (Mark 2; Luke 5). Whoever he is, let him choose which he wishes: either let him confess the Holy Spirit, who forgives sins, to be God in all respects, or, if he does not believe that pardon of sins can be granted through him, he has emptied in himself the benefit of regeneration and the sacrament of baptism. It belongs, then, to God alone to loose what is bound, to restore what is corrupted, to cleanse what is stained. And therefore, conscious of our weakness and of his majesty, we cry out to him with groaning: Against you alone have I sinned (Ps. 50), Lord, who alone are not held by the law of sin, who alone are a stranger to it not in act but by nature, and therefore alone can absolve debtors, who alone are free of debts, who have not borrowed what you have from elsewhere, but are full of your own. For no one gave to you first, nor are you watered by powers drawn from elsewhere, nor has any transfusion been made into you from any other; but you yourself are the source of your own river, and your glory is your nature; as it knows no beginning, so it has received nothing from one before it (John 14; Rom. 8; Luke 17).
CHAPTER VIII.
Where it is shown that the temple of God is the temple of the Holy Spirit.

The sacred words define the Spirit properly as the indweller of the human heart: The Father, it says, will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you for ever (1 Cor. 3; 1 Cor. 6). And to the Romans: He will give life also to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you. And therefore we rightly understand what was written of the Holy Spirit: The kingdom of God is within you. They are indeed the kingdom of God who deserve to obey him, [made] into a temple of God, certainly, not of a creature. Hear through the Apostle the voice of our indweller: You are, he says, the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. And in another place, as God says: I will dwell in them, and walk among them, and I will be their God. See, he himself who inhabits the temple of the human heart declares himself to be God. Ananias, among those who, honouring God, sold their possessions from their just labours and laid [the proceeds] before the feet of the apostles, is recognised to have promised a vow to God, [yet] is charged with having lied to the Holy Spirit, as the apostle Peter says: Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit (Acts 3)? And going on he added: You have not lied to men, but to God. What is this? He sins against the Creator, and does Scripture so lessen his sin as to make it, according to the sense of impiety, an offence against a creature, and assign him as debtor to a lesser being for an insult to a greater? It is not so. He to whom the offence of sacrilege is referred is manifestly endowed with divine power, he of whom it says in another place: But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not have forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the one to come (Matt. 11). Since, then, he tempted God by his transgression, he is said to have deceived the Holy Spirit. Therefore recognise one cause, one glory, one reverence of the Holy Spirit and of God. And so he concludes most evidently about the Holy Spirit in the following words: You have not, he says, lied to men, but to God. While Peter was speaking to Cornelius, the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out even upon the nations (Acts 10). You see that the Holy Spirit bestowed not from what belonged to another, but from his own. If you ask who this is who gave them grace: God. This bestower of grace [Scripture] declared above specifically to be the Holy Spirit, here to be God. There by a proper name, here by a common name, the confession is proved by repetition. And when it says that the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out even upon the nations, he who is the author of grace is God by nature. It belongs to God alone to bestow the gifts of the spiritual gifts from his own, so that the Apostle too may be seen to have said of him: I laboured more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me (1 Cor. 15). Rightly is he declared God who is the dispenser of grace and of human salvation. And Peter added: Who was I, that I could hinder God (Acts 11)? That God, certainly, who poured the onrush of overflowing grace upon the nations, or upon Cornelius.
CHAPTER IX.
Where, against the Novatians, God gave the Gentiles repentance unto life, and this God is shown by the very order of the reading to be the Holy Spirit.

Notice how, in the person of the Holy Spirit, who suddenly filled Cornelius and his companions, the name of God is celebrated with manifold attestation. Having heard these things, it says, they were silent, and glorified God, saying: So God has given repentance unto life to the Gentiles too (Acts 11)? In this place it must be noted against the Novatians that he is said to give repentance, which he certainly bestows in no other way than through the ministry of his servants. So when it says: Who was I, that I could hinder God; and again: So God has given repentance unto life to the Gentiles, what interpretation need be made plain in things that are plain, when the confession of the divine name, repeated so many times at the coming of the Holy Spirit, would not satisfy either the ignorant or the unbelieving?
CHAPTER X.
Where, in First Corinthians, the Holy Spirit is declared to be God by the distributions of powers.

Take [what is said] to the Corinthians, which alone could suffice to assert the divinity of the Holy Spirit. He says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: God bearing witness by signs and wonders and various powers, and by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will (Heb. 2). Let us ask the apostle himself whether this distributor of spiritual gifts is one of the creatures. We have in First Corinthians: I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says anathema to Jesus. And no one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12). Notice how here he has most absolutely designated the Spirit of God to be the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit whom in the preceding sentence he put forward as the Spirit of God speaking. Clearly the following [words] testify how manifestly he is God and Lord. There are, he says, divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God. As if the blessed apostle had been consulted about the divinity of the Holy Spirit, of him of whom he had said, the same Spirit, he evidently adds: the same God, who works all things in all. He could not work all things if he were one among all things. Here recognise the Holy Spirit, as much in his own name as in [that of] Lord and God, either clearly expressed, or certainly joined to the Trinity. But here, in the divisions of gifts, the divine word is understood rather to have designated the Holy Spirit, because above we learn that the grace of distributions belongs to the Holy Spirit by a special dispensation. And what he said: the same Lord, but the same God, he shows in the following passage must be referred to the Holy Spirit, saying: To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in the one Spirit, to another the working of powers, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of speech; but all these one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each as he wills. He is subject to no one, but is the heavenly Lord, who bestows heavenly gifts by his own will and by the right of his power.
CHAPTER XI.
It must be noted that just as he speaks of one God, so he speaks of one Holy Spirit, which could in no way be said of a common creature, nor that it divides to each as it wills.

You see that just as there is one Father and one Son, so also there is one Holy Spirit, as he consequently assigns: For in one Spirit we have been given to drink. If he were of the common crowd or of the multitude of creation, he could not at all be called one. And since you have here: to another, he says, is given faith in the same Spirit (Rom. 12), who bestows this faith the same Apostle declared to the Corinthians, saying: And to each as God has divided the measure of faith (Heb.). You see that he declares without doubt that this divider of faith is God. Although in so manifold a bounty of such great gifts the very magnificence of the work by itself speaks the power of its author, yet he concluded about him thus: But all these one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each as he wills. As also in another place: The Spirit blows where he wills. And again: And by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will (1 Cor. 12). This, then, is not [the part] of a servitude subjected to ministries, but the choice of free power, and in the distributions of heavenly goods the goodness of the highest bounty is poured out in full. As it says, and by distributions of the Holy Spirit: this distributor, that is, divider, whether he is God, he taught the Corinthians, saying: And there are divisions of operations, but the same God. We read in the Acts of the Apostles: Take heed, it says, to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has set you as bishops to rule the Church of God (Acts 20). He who set bishops in the Church, the Vessel of election declares to the Corinthians to be God, saying thus: Some indeed God has set in the Church. Who are these but the Holy Spirit, whose personal office the distribution of graces shows, as follows in the continuous passage? God has set, he says, in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then graces of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues. Some, he says, God has set in the Church. That here he said God of the Holy Spirit, the very dispensation of sanctifications and powers that belongs to the Holy Spirit makes plain. For he enriches the mouths of the prophets, dispenses the remedies of healings, multiplies the ornaments of the spiritual gifts; and as he flowed into the apostles, the miracles of signs and the diverse kinds of tongues proclaimed him to be the God of the universe.
CHAPTER XII.
Where he says that those who have been made the temple of the Holy Spirit ought so to advance that they may be worthy to carry God in the body.

So the Apostle says to the Corinthians: Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Spirit? That the temple of the Holy Spirit is the temple of God the preceding parts of the same Epistle clearly indicate, when it is said: Or do you not know that you are the temple of God? and the Holy Spirit dwells in you; and the Spirit, it says, of God dwells in you. Who would doubt that they are the temple of that God whose dwelling-place they are proved to be? And when he had said: Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, he concluded the passage with shining truth thus: Glorify, he says, and carry God in your body. Therefore he who zealously prepares in his heart a temple of purity for the Holy Spirit carries God in his body through chastity and the mortification of the flesh. We must carry bodily him by whom we are spiritually possessed. Therefore know that he whom you see worthy of a temple is to be adored with divine honours, celebrated with vows, worshipped with sacrifices. So the teacher of the Gentiles speaks to the universal Church: Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you? This is possible for no creature, but it is the mark of divine majesty, that it fills peoples individually through each one, and yet remains in the immensity of its fullness. It is, he says, singular to and proper of the divine nature to be present in all places, to enter into all things and to contain all things. It is peculiar to God, he says, to strip the sons of perdition of the debts of nature, to renew them with cleansed consciences, to make them sons of God, and to raise them up into the glory of the heavenly kingdom.
